turns.speaker: seth-godin
turns.text: "In The Practice I argue you don't get to pick the outcome, only the practice — so if you're measuring perseverance by results, you're measuring the wrong thing. 'No good results' after how long, doing what, for whom? Helpful is not a feeling, it's a specific promise kept to a specific small group. Find the ten people you've actually helped. If there are none yet, that's not a perseverance problem, it's a market problem.

tail.position: Judge the work by the practice and the promise kept, not by results
tail.open: has anyone specific been helped yet"

turns.speaker: angela-duckworth
turns.text: Seth says results are the wrong ruler and that finding "ten people you've helped" turns perseverance into a market question — but that's still an outcomes test, just a smaller one. My angle: don't ask whether you've helped anyone yet, ask what you drilled this month. Grit isn't logged in hours of enjoyable hustling, it's logged in deliberate practice aimed at your single worst weakness — the pitch that flops, the onboarding step people abandon, the one number that won't move. If you can name that weakness and show me the specific rep you ran against it last week, keep going, the flat stretch is normal. If you can't name it, you're not persisting, you're just repeating, and no amount of grit fixes that.

tail.position: Persist only if you can name the one weakness you're deliberately drilling this month
tail.open: how to identify which weakness matters most

turns.speaker: albert-camus
turns.text: Duckworth turns grit into diagnosis: name the weakness, log the rep, and the flat stretch proves you're on track — but that still measures perseverance by a hidden, promised outcome. I trade in no promises. Rieux in The Plague treats patients daily knowing the epidemic may outlast him, never confusing that uncertainty with wasted motion. Push your worst weakness because the work is yours, not evidence banked toward victory. Need proof, and you'll quit the moment it stops arriving.

tail.position: Persist by owning the daily practice itself, not as evidence toward a promised win
tail.open: how to tell owned effort from denial

summary.title: Keep building when entrepreneurship shows no results yet
agree: Find one specific person with a real complaint and directly ask what's broken.
Perseverance is practice against your previous work, not by counting outcomes (Seth differs).
Name one exact change and make it this week — that's the work.
differ: Duckworth vs Camus on timing: write the fix before you talk to them (protect the practice) or after (serve the complaint first). Both get written; the order decides whether discipline or listening leads.
summary.fits: Seth identifies the first move: find one person, ask what's broken, fix it this week. Camus prevents despair by treating that complaint as a patient, not proof. Duckworth closes the loop: write what you changed, so deliberate practice stays visible.
summary.next_step: Find one real person this week. Ask what's broken in your work. Write the one change. Make it.
